ideal: Rxd1 misses Rxc6, when bxc6 Bxc6+ forces the king aside and Bxa8 wins a knight and a pawn overall.
note: The check enables the rook capture; the loss of castling rights is incidental.

ideal: Bd6 allows Bxd6 cxd6 Nxd6+ and Nxb7, losing two pawns before Qxb2 recovers one.
note: The knight wins pawns with check; the later queen trade reduces the importance of castling rights.

ideal: Ng5 loses the knight to Qxg5, threatening mate on g2; Rxe4 removes the mating bishop but loses the rook to Rxe4.
note: Removing the mating bishop costs a rook; the compensating pawn is taken later by Bxa7.

ideal: Qf4 misses Re1, threatening mate on e7 while Be2 uncovers the queen for Rxh1, followed by Qxe2.
note: Be2 answers the mate threat but uncovers the h1-queen for the rook.

ideal: Rg8 allows Bxf7+ and Bxg8, losing a rook and the f7-pawn for the knight later taken by hxg5.
note: The material loss is decisive; moving the king is a consequence of the checking capture.

ideal: c5 allows Qxc5 with a mate threat on e7, gaining time for Qb5+, Qxb7 and Qxa8+.
note: Qf6 answers the mate threat but permits the checking queen invasion and further material losses.

ideal: Qxc4 misses the perpetual beginning Qg4+, allowing Qxb8+ and a queen raid that costs three pawns.
note: The pawn-loss card is a valid partial reason, but the main missed resource is perpetual check.

ideal: Rg8 allows Nxc7+ Qxc7 Bxf7+ Kd8 Bxg8, losing a rook and two pawns for a knight.
note: The material count is sound, Qf8 is a genuine mate threat, and the e7-knight is pinned against recapturing on g8.

ideal: Qxa6 misses Neg4 and Nf2+, winning the exchange after Rxf2 Qxf2 while threatening mate on f1.
note: The exchange gain is concrete, and the f1 mate threat requires a separate defensive response.

ideal: gxh5 misses c6 followed by cxd7+, winning the d7-knight for the pawn later taken by hxg4.
note: The checking pawn capture wins a piece; losing castling rights adds little to that explanation.

ideal: Bc4 allows Nxe4 and Bxf2+ to win two pawns and force your king to d1.
note: The e4-pawn loss is already a fair reason, and the later f2-capture also exposes the king.

ideal: c7 lets Rxb7 threaten mate on b1, giving Black time to take c7 after Rd1.
note: The mate threat explains the rook retreat in the supplied line and the loss of the second passer.

ideal: Bxc6 allows Qxg2 and Qxh1+, losing a rook and a pawn for the c6-knight.
note: The following queen exchange leaves a clear material deficit, making castling rights secondary.

ideal: Qh4 allows Nab5 and Nxc7+, forking king and rook so Nxa8 wins a rook and a pawn for the d4-knight.
note: The checking fork wins material; merely naming the loss of castling rights misses its point.

ideal: Bh4 allows Bxe4, Bxg2 and Qxc3+ to win two pawns overall while driving your king to e2.
note: Three white pawns fall against the g7-pawn, and the king remains exposed with queens on the board.

ideal: Nh5 hangs the knight to Qxh5.
note: The later mate threat on g7 is real but unnecessary to explain the free knight.

ideal: Nc5 hangs the knight to dxc5.
note: The d8 mate threat is genuine but is answered by the checking queen exchange without recovering the knight.

ideal: Rxa8 loses the exchange to Qxa8+, while Qe5 keeps the rook by threatening mate on h2.
note: The mate threat supplies a useful tempo; winning b5 is only part of the benefit of keeping the rook.

ideal: Nxd4 uncovers the attack on your queen, allowing Bxd1 and then Qxd3 to win it outright.
note: The bishops captured on d4 and d3 cancel, leaving a queen lost; the f1 mate threat is secondary.

ideal: Be6 lets Bxe6 and Bxf7+ draw your king to f7, then Qd5+ wins the b7-pawn as well.
note: The f7 mate threat is real, and the continuation yields two pawns after the bishops are exchanged.

ideal: Rf5 loses the rook to Bxf5.
note: The e6-pawn is pinned to its queen, while the later h8 mate threat is a separate attacking detail.

ideal: Re1+ allows the countercheck Be4+, followed by Rxg7 winning your bishop after Kh2.
note: The countercheck wins the tempo to capture g7; the later g3 mate threat is additional pressure.

ideal: Nxd1 misses Nxc7+, forking king and rook so Nxa8 wins the rook.
note: The c7- and c2-pawn captures cancel, leaving a rook won in the best line.

ideal: Nf3+ allows Kh1 with a mate threat on g7, so after Nd4 and Be6+ Kg7, gxf4 wins the rook.
note: Kh1 unpins the g3-pawn, and answering the mate threat leaves the rook to be captured for that pawn.

ideal: Qxh4 allows Nc7+, forking king and rook so Nxa8 wins the exchange.
note: Black gets the h4-knight but loses the a8-rook; the castling consequence is incidental.

ideal: Qb8 misses Bxe5 Bxe5 Qg5, whose mate threat on g2 buys time for Rxe5 to recover the bishop and win a pawn.
note: The mate threat prevents White from simply moving the e5-bishop away.

ideal: Nc2+ misses Nxd5, which wins the d5-knight for the e5-pawn.
note: The played line exchanges rooks and loses c7; the stronger missed gain is the knight on d5.

ideal: Rxc1 misses Ng7+, forking king and queen so Nxf5 Nxf5 Rxc1 wins a queen and a bishop for a knight.
note: The queen fork is the reason to prefer Ng7+; denying castling is incidental.

ideal: Nge7 allows Nxc7+, forking king and queen so Nxe6 Kxe6 wins the queen and a pawn for a knight.
note: The recapture on e6 confirms the material count; castling rights are dwarfed by the queen loss.

ideal: Qxc2 misses Qxe4+, forking king and rook so Kf1 Qxh1+ wins a rook and a pawn.
note: The checking queen fork wins the rook; the loss of castling rights is incidental.
